title: SYSK Selects: How Silly Putty Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2011 episode "How Silly Putty Works." Josh introduces it as a best-of pick. The hosts trace rubber history from Charles Goodyear's vulcanization (1839) through the Amazon rubber boom, British seeding of Southeast Asian plantations, and WWII synthetic rubber (GR-S). They cover James Wright of General Electric inventing the bouncing putty from boric acid and silicone oil, and Peter Hodgson's 1950 marketing of it through Block toy store, Neiman Marcus and Doubleday bookshops, boosted by a New Yorker Talk of the Town piece. They discuss the product's odd properties, viscosity and non-Newtonian fluid behavior, a listener email on non-Newtonian fluids, and a homemade recipe using Elmer's glue, borax and warm water. A listener email on the dumbing-down of culture closes the episode.
topics: New Yorker Talk of the Town
rubber tree seeds Britain Southeast Asia

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Saturday Select episode on how Silly Putty works, originally aired October 2011, and the hosts banter about their appearance and beards.

segments.title: Rubber history: vulcanization, Amazon boom and Southeast Asia
segments.summary: Charles Goodyear's 1839 vulcanization made rubber tougher, driving demand during the Industrial Revolution. Brazil and the Amazon dominated the rubber trade until British agents took rubber tree seeds to London, and Southeast Asian colonies took over the market by 1920.
topics: rubber tree seeds Britain Southeast Asia

segments.title: WWII rubber shortage and GR-S synthetic rubber
segments.summary: Japan's invasion of Southeast Asia cut off US rubber supply in WWII. The War Production Board called for synthetic rubber, leading to GR-S, which became the standard and out-produced the world's natural rubber combined.

segments.title: Invention by James Wright at General Electric
segments.summary: James Wright of General Electric mixed boric acid with silicone oil to create a bouncing putty that was not a useful rubber substitute. It was passed around to other labs for about a decade.

segments.title: Peter Hodgson, Block toy store and early marketing
segments.summary: Peter Hodgson, an ad agency owner in New Haven, saw the putty at a New Year's Eve party and worked with Ruth Fallgatter of the Block toy store to sell it in its catalog for two dollars as an adult diversion. Hodgson later bought a batch from GE, packaged it in plastic eggs, reverse-engineered it, opened a plant in Connecticut and landed Neiman Marcus and Doubleday.

segments.title: New Yorker article and sales boom
segments.summary: A New Yorker Talk of the Town piece about Doubleday selling Silly Putty caused sales to explode, with about a quarter million orders in three days. Hodgson died in 1976 with sales above five million a year in 22 countries. Kids came to dominate sales, and the hosts discuss copying newsprint and comics.
topics: New Yorker Talk of the Town

segments.title: Silly Putty properties and fluid science
segments.summary: The hosts describe Silly Putty's stretch, snap, slow flow and high bounce. They explain viscosity, measured in pascal seconds and poise, and how temperature affects viscous fluids, distinguishing Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. The main ingredient is polydimethylsiloxane, a viscoelastic polymer.

segments.title: Listener email on non-Newtonian fluids
segments.summary: A young listener named Matthew from New York explains non-Newtonian fluids using cornstarch and water, and the hosts praise the explanation.

segments.title: Making homemade Silly Putty
segments.summary: The hosts give a recipe using white glue, warm water, borax and food coloring. Borax links the glue's polymer chains into a web, making the putty elastic. They note it can be stored in a sealed bag or the fridge and advise adult supervision.

segments.title: Listener email on dumbing down of culture and corrections
segments.summary: Listener Josephine discusses the so-called dumbing down of culture and the value of internet research. The hosts also correct the Cheddar cheese origin and give contact information.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Sign-off with contact information and website reference.
